prompt_free_text:
This paper studies an important and timely problem: how to obtain formal privacy guarantees when aligning LLM behavior via activation steering using private demonstrations. The core proposal, PSA, is simple and appealing: compute steering vectors from positive/negative demonstration pairs, clip per-example activation differences, add Gaussian noise, and then use the privatized steering vectors at inference time. The paper also introduces a membership inference attack tailored to activation editing and evaluates utility/privacy tradeoffs across several models and behavioral benchmarks. Overall, I found the paper interesting, relevant, and potentially impactful, especially because activation editing is increasingly used as a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning, yet its privacy implications have been largely ignored.

The main strength of the paper is the problem formulation itself. Privacy for activation steering is indeed underexplored, and the observation that steering vectors derived from private demonstrations may leak membership or sensitive attributes is well motivated. The proposed solution is conceptually clean and leverages standard differential privacy machinery in a natural way. The offline nature of the release is also practically attractive: once a privatized steering vector is produced, arbitrarily many downstream generations can be served without additional privacy cost by post-processing. This is a meaningful distinction from many interactive private inference settings. I also appreciate that the paper does not stop at formal guarantees, but attempts empirical privacy auditing via a custom MIA.

The empirical scope is another positive aspect. The paper evaluates multiple model families and sizes, several alignment-related behaviors, and includes not only behavioral accuracy but also open-ended generation quality and a general-capability check via MMLU. The scaling observation—that larger models appear to incur smaller utility degradation under the same steering privatization—is interesting and potentially useful for practitioners. The MIA section is also a valuable addition, since privacy papers that only state formal DP guarantees without any empirical audit often leave open the question of whether the threat is meaningful in practice.

That said, I have several substantive concerns, some of which affect correctness and some of which affect the strength of the empirical claims.

My biggest concern is the DP accounting and mechanism specification. The paper states that after clipping/scaling, the per-layer steering vector is released as the average plus isotropic Gaussian noise with standard deviation sigma = 2 sqrt(2 ln(1.25/delta)) / (n epsilon). However, the clipping rule in Algorithm 1 appears inconsistent with the surrounding text and with standard sensitivity analysis. The text says vectors are projected to an L2 ball of radius C_l and then scaled by C_l, but the formula given is d_i^l / max{C_l, ||d_i^l||_2}. This maps vectors to norm at most 1/C_l times the original when ||d_i^l|| <= C_l? More precisely, if ||d_i^l|| <= C_l, the output is d_i^l / C_l, not d_i^l; if ||d_i^l|| > C_l, the output is d_i^l / ||d_i^l||, i.e., norm 1. So the operation is not “clip to radius C_l” but rather “normalize by max(C_l, norm),” yielding outputs of norm at most 1. That may be fine, but then the text should say so clearly. More importantly, the sensitivity constant of the average depends on whether neighboring datasets are defined by add/remove or replace-one adjacency, and on the exact norm bound after preprocessing. The factor of 2 in sigma suggests replace-one adjacency with per-example norm bound 1, but this is not explicitly justified. Since the privacy theorem is central, the paper needs a precise proposition with proof, including the adjacency notion, the exact sensitivity derivation, and whether the Gaussian noise is added coordinate-wise with covariance sigma^2 I_d. As written, the privacy section is intuitive but not rigorous enough for a top-tier venue.

Relatedly, the composition discussion is somewhat underdeveloped. The paper allocates per-layer privacy epsilon_l and reports total epsilon as five times epsilon_l for five layers, which is fine under basic composition, but the presentation is confusing because Algorithm 1 is parameterized by epsilon, delta while Table 2 reports per-layer and total values without clearly stating whether the same noise scale is used across all layers and datasets. The implementation section says “The noisy vectors are generated by adding Gaussian noise with 0.02 standard deviation. We fix delta = 1/(5n). This gives us the theoretical epsilon...” This sounds like epsilon is derived post hoc from a fixed sigma, rather than sigma being calibrated from a target epsilon. That is acceptable, but then the method is not really “given epsilon, add calibrated noise”; it is “given sigma, infer epsilon.” The paper should be explicit and consistent about whether privacy is target-driven or noise-driven. Also, because activation dimension d can be large, it would be useful to clarify whether the stated sigma is per-coordinate and whether any dependence on d enters utility but not privacy.

A second major concern is that the empirical evaluation, while broad, is not statistically convincing in its current form. The paper repeatedly claims “comparable performance” and “minimal utility loss,” but there are no confidence intervals, standard deviations across noise draws, or significance tests. Since PSA is randomized, reporting a single run can be misleading. This is especially important because some of the reported gains/losses appear small and could easily fall within variance due to sampling, decoding randomness, or the DP noise itself. At minimum, the paper should average over multiple independent noise realizations and report uncertainty. This applies to behavioral accuracy, GPT-4 judged scores, and MMLU. Without this, it is difficult to assess whether PSA truly preserves utility or whether the observed differences are incidental.

The use of GPT-4 as evaluator is reasonable as a supplementary signal, but the presentation of Table 3 raises questions. The scores are very low for some behaviors (e.g., around 0.15–0.18 for AI Coordination) and clustered tightly for others, yet the paper interprets these as evidence of similar quality. It is unclear what exactly these numbers measure, how prompts were designed, whether the judge was blinded to method, and how robust the judgments are. Since the paper’s main utility claim partly relies on these evaluations, more methodological detail and variance estimates are needed. Human evaluation would be ideal, but if not feasible, at least stronger LLM-as-a-judge protocols should be described.

There are also issues with the baselines. The paper compares PSA mainly to mean steering and PCA steering, plus zero-shot. This is a reasonable starting point, but for a privacy paper I would expect stronger comparisons to alternative privatization strategies. For example, what happens if one simply subsamples demonstrations, uses public demonstrations only, or adds noise to activations at inference rather than to the steering vector? Even if these alternatives do not provide the same formal guarantee, they would help contextualize the privacy-utility tradeoff. More importantly, since the paper claims to be the first DP method for activation editing, it would be useful to compare against a straightforward DP variant of PCA steering as well, or at least explain why mean steering is the only method privatized.

The MIA section is promising but currently somewhat narrow. The attack is based on synthetic canaries inserted into demonstrations and then detecting whether the steered model preferentially emits the target canary given the anchor. This is a sensible first attack, but it is closer to a canary extraction or targeted membership test than a general-purpose MIA over natural examples. The paper should be more careful in its framing. The attack demonstrates that steering vectors can encode and reveal rare associations, which is valuable, but it does not fully establish privacy risk for ordinary demonstration membership. Also, the threshold tau is chosen differently for different models, apparently manually, and the attack uses 100 generations at temperature 0.8. This gives the adversary substantial query access and tuning freedom; that may be acceptable, but the protocol should be justified and sensitivity to tau, temperature, and number of samples should be reported. Otherwise, the empirical epsilon estimates may be fragile.

On empirical epsilon, I appreciate the attempt to connect attack success rates to privacy auditing, but the interpretation should be more cautious. The formula used gives a lower bound or empirical estimate associated with a specific adversary and test, not a general privacy guarantee. Saying that empirical epsilon is smaller than theoretical epsilon and therefore “privacy is better protected” is directionally fine, but the paper should emphasize that this only reflects the tested attack family and setup. In particular, the non-private mean steering having finite “empirical epsilon” does not mean it satisfies DP with that epsilon; it only means this attack achieved that operating point. The distinction between formal DP and attack-specific auditing should be stated more sharply.

Another concern is the realism of the private-data setting and the chosen datasets. The seven behavioral datasets are useful for steering evaluation, but they are not obviously private in the sense motivating the paper (healthcare, finance, etc.). The paper’s privacy motivation is about sensitive user records, yet the experiments use public alignment benchmarks with synthetic privacy assumptions. This is understandable for reproducibility, but it weakens the practical claim. A stronger paper would include at least one more realistic private-domain dataset or a simulation where demonstrations contain sensitive attributes embedded in otherwise task-relevant prompts/completions. As is, the paper convincingly shows that one can privatize steering on benchmark behaviors, but less convincingly that this solves the motivating real-world problem.

I also found some presentation and correctness issues in the algorithms and tables. In Algorithm 1, the difference vector formula appears to have a typo: d_i^l = h_l((p, c^+)) - h_l((p_i, c_i^-)) should presumably use p_i, c_i^+ in the first term. There are several formatting artifacts and duplicated figure blocks. Table 5 appears incomplete, with the zero-shot row truncated. These may be draft issues, but they make it harder to verify the claims. More importantly, the paper should specify the selected layers for each model and behavior, how C_l is chosen, whether lambda is tuned on validation data, and whether the same hyperparameters are used for PSA and non-private steering. Since clipping thresholds can materially affect both utility and privacy, their selection procedure is crucial.

The scaling claim is interesting but currently under-supported. Figure 4 appears to focus only on the Refusal dataset and Qwen sizes. From that, the paper extrapolates a broader rule that larger LLMs exhibit stronger privacy-utility tradeoffs. This may be true, but the evidence is limited. I would encourage the authors to either soften the claim or expand the analysis across more behaviors and perhaps more than one model family. It would also be useful to disentangle whether the effect comes from stronger base alignment in larger models, lower sensitivity of activations, or simply higher zero-shot performance leaving less room for degradation.

One conceptual point worth discussing more is what exactly is protected by DP here. The released object is a steering vector computed from demonstration pairs. DP protects membership of individual demonstrations under the chosen adjacency relation. However, if the demonstrations themselves encode aggregate sensitive properties or if the steering vector intentionally captures a rare concept strongly associated with a subgroup, DP does not prevent all downstream harms. This is not a flaw of the method, but the paper could better articulate the scope and limits of the guarantee. In particular, because the steering vector is reused for infinitely many queries, the post-processing argument is correct, but only insofar as the vector itself is the sole data-dependent release. Any hyperparameter tuning on private data, layer selection, threshold selection, or prompt-template adaptation would also need to be accounted for if done privately. The current exposition risks giving the impression that the whole pipeline is DP even if some choices may have been informed by private data.

Despite these concerns, I think the paper has a solid core idea and could become a strong contribution with revisions. The novelty is meaningful, the method is simple and likely useful, and the empirical results are encouraging. My overall assessment is positive but not unequivocal because the current version falls short on rigor in the privacy analysis and on statistical robustness in the experiments.

The most important improvements I would request are the following. First, provide a formal theorem and proof for the privacy guarantee of PSA, with exact preprocessing definition, adjacency notion, sensitivity derivation, and composition accounting. Second, clean up the algorithmic description and implementation details, especially the role of C_l, sigma, epsilon, and layer selection. Third, rerun the main experiments over multiple random seeds/noise draws and report uncertainty intervals. Fourth, strengthen the MIA evaluation with ablations over threshold, number of generations, and perhaps a more natural-example attack or at least a clearer framing of the canary attack’s scope. Fifth, improve the discussion of limitations and the exact scope of the DP guarantee.

In summary, this is a novel and practically relevant paper on a neglected privacy problem in activation steering. The proposed approach is elegant and the initial evidence is promising. However, the current manuscript needs stronger technical precision and more careful empirical methodology before I would consider it fully convincing at a top-tier conference. My leaning is weak accept if the venue values novelty and emerging directions, but there are enough rigor issues that a weak reject would also be understandable.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper studies privacy-preserving activation steering for LLM alignment. It proposes PSA, which computes per-layer steering vectors from paired positive/negative demonstrations, clips per-example activation differences, and adds Gaussian noise to obtain differentially private steering vectors. The paper argues that once these vectors are privately released, they can be reused for arbitrarily many inference queries by post-processing. Empirically, PSA is evaluated on seven alignment-related benchmarks across several open-source LLM families and sizes, with comparisons to zero-shot, mean steering, and PCA steering. The paper also introduces a canary-based membership inference attack tailored to activation steering and reports reduced attack success under PSA.
strengths: Addresses a novel and important problem: privacy risks in activation steering for LLM alignment have received little prior attention.
The core idea is simple, practical, and computationally lightweight compared with DP fine-tuning approaches.
The privacy framing is appealing: privatize the steering vectors once offline, then reuse them at inference time without additional privacy cost.
Experiments span multiple model families, sizes, and several alignment-relevant behaviors, suggesting some breadth of applicability.
The paper attempts both theoretical privacy guarantees and empirical privacy auditing via a tailored membership inference attack.
Results suggest PSA often preserves much of the utility of non-private steering while improving empirical resistance to the proposed attack.
weaknesses: The DP mechanism and its presentation are mathematically imprecise in several places, weakening confidence in the claimed guarantees.

The clipping/scaling rule in Algorithm 1 is unusual and insufficiently justified; the notation suggests normalization to norm at most 1, but the role of the threshold C_l and resulting sensitivity are not derived carefully.

Noise calibration appears inconsistent between theory and experiments: the algorithm defines sigma from epsilon, delta, and n, while experiments instead fix a noise standard deviation of 0.02 and back out epsilon. This disconnect makes it hard to assess whether the implemented method matches the theoretical mechanism.
The Gaussian mechanism is written as adding N(0, sigma^2) to a vector output without specifying isotropic multivariate noise; this is a nontrivial omission for a vector-valued release.
The empirical evaluation relies heavily on figures/tables without sufficient statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance across random seeds/noise draws are reported.
The MIA evaluation is narrow, using only the hallucination dataset and two models, with attack thresholds apparently hand-tuned per model, limiting the strength of privacy conclusions.
Some reported utility gains of PSA over non-private steering are attributed to noise helping, but this is speculative and not systematically analyzed.
Evaluation of open-ended generation uses GPT-4 as judge without human validation or robustness checks, and some reported absolute scores are difficult to interpret.
The MMLU table appears incomplete/malformed, which raises concerns about result reporting quality.
methodological_flaws: Algorithm 1 likely contains a notation/error bug: d_i^l is defined as h_l((p,c^+)) - h_l((p_i,c_i^-)) instead of h_l((p_i,c_i^+)) - h_l((p_i,c_i^-)). If this is not merely typographical, the method is ill-defined.

The sensitivity argument is not fully correct as written. After clipping/normalization, each per-example vector has norm at most 1, so replacing one record changes the average by at most 2/n. However, the paper does not explicitly derive this under its exact clipping rule, nor clarify whether neighboring datasets are replace-one or add/remove-one. The chosen sigma depends on this distinction.

The Gaussian mechanism statement is simplified to sigma = Delta_f * sqrt(2 ln(1.25/delta)) / epsilon, which is only a standard sufficient bound under particular parameter regimes; the paper treats it as exact and does not discuss dimensionality or multivariate noise specification.

Composition accounting is weak. The paper uses basic composition over layers and claims it is tighter for fewer than 5 layers, but Table 2 uses 5 layers exactly and no formal comparison is shown. More importantly, if hyperparameters/layers are selected using private data, that selection itself would consume privacy budget; this issue is not addressed.

The claim that the method can answer an infinite number of queries with no extra privacy cost is only valid if the only private object released is the DP steering vector and all subsequent tuning/selection uses no private feedback. The paper does not clearly separate these assumptions from the actual experimental workflow.

Experimental privacy auditing does not validate the DP guarantee in a strong sense. The empirical epsilon computed from one specific attack is only a lower-bound-style audit of vulnerability to that attack, not evidence that the mechanism satisfies a tighter privacy guarantee in general. The discussion risks overstating what empirical epsilon means.
The attack threshold tau is manually chosen per model, which may bias attack performance. There is no clear train/validation/test separation for attack calibration.
The paper does not report robustness across multiple noise realizations for PSA. Since DP noise is central to the method, single-run results can be misleading.

Using fixed noise std 0.02 across datasets/models while claiming dataset-specific epsilon values suggests the practical mechanism may not be consistently calibrated to the stated privacy target, especially if clipping thresholds C_l vary or are not reported.

The utility comparisons may be confounded by unreported choices of selected layers, clipping thresholds, and steering strengths. Since these hyperparameters strongly affect steering performance, lack of transparent tuning protocol reduces empirical validity.
